A systematic review of 50 naturalistic classroom studies identified learner responses to WCF as one of four major themes, and noted that most included studies adopted qualitative designs (66.0%) and that only 11 (22.0%) made explicit reference to theoretical tenets (Mao et al., 2024).

The same study reported that cognitive load during revision was significantly lower after direct corrections on grammatical errors than after metalinguistic codes on grammatical and non-grammatical errors (Bonilla López et al., 2018).

Automated feedback occupies a different position in the revision process. Zhang and Hyland (2018) found that automated writing evaluation tended to flag rather than correct errors, and that teacher feedback addressed more error types than the automated system, although differing assignment demands may have confounded the comparison. In an integrated classroom case study, the majority of 33 students actively engaged with combined automated, peer, and teacher feedback, and the approach promoted behavioural, affective, and cognitive engagement and encouraged thoughtful revisions (Zhang & Hyland, 2021). The same authors note that students were not required to address all feedback received (Zhang & Hyland, 2021).

The design is unusually strong for this literature—random assignment, a genuine control, and a delayed posttest—but the single Costa Rican university setting and the self-report measure of cognitive load limit what can be claimed about other proficiency levels and contexts.

The finding that direct corrections imposed significantly lower cognitive load than metalinguistic codes offers a plausible mechanism for the durability difference, yet the authors acknowledge they could not employ an online physiological measure, so the load account remains inferential.

sentences: Research on how second-language (L2) writers revise after written corrective feedback (WCF) converges on a distinction between the accuracy gains that different feedback forms produce during revision and those they sustain beyond it.

Bonilla López et al. (2018) tested this directly: 139 low-intermediate EFL writers were randomly assigned to direct corrections, metalinguistic codes, or a self-correction control, and although both coded and direct feedback improved immediate grammatical and non-grammatical accuracy during revision, only direct corrections retained an advantage four weeks later.

The design is unusually strong for this literature—random assignment, a genuine control, and a delayed posttest—but the single Costa Rican university setting and the self-report measure of cognitive load limit what can be claimed about other proficiency levels and contexts.

The finding that direct corrections imposed significantly lower cognitive load than metalinguistic codes offers a plausible mechanism for the durability difference, yet the authors acknowledge they could not employ an online physiological measure, so the load account remains inferential.
Automated feedback complicates this picture.

Zhang and Hyland (2018) found that automated writing evaluation tended to flag rather than correct errors, and that teacher feedback addressed more error types than the automated system, although differing assignment demands may have confounded the comparison.

Their case study is instructive precisely because engagement varied so widely—one learner resubmitted thirteen times while the other resubmitted once—but two students in one semester cannot support generalisation.

A larger integrated-feedback case study reported that most of 33 students engaged actively with combined automated, peer, and teacher feedback and made thoughtful revisions (Zhang & Hyland, 2021), though the authors concede that nothing required students to address the feedback they received, leaving uptake partly voluntary.

More recent work on prompt design suggests automated systems can detect errors with high precision but that recall rises steeply with prompt sophistication, from 10% to 55% (Luo et al., 2025); this indicates that automated feedback quality is a design variable rather than a fixed property, though the 30-essay corpus from one institution constrains generalisation.
Synthesis across these studies is hampered by divergent outcome measures—accuracy scores, revision operations, resubmission counts—and by the predominance of single-site designs.

What we know is that feedback form shapes both the accuracy of revision and its persistence; what we do not know is how these effects interact with learner proficiency and engagement over extended classroom use.

uncited_sentences.sentence: Research on how second-language writers revise after written corrective feedback (WCF) converges on a distinction between immediate text improvement and durable accuracy gains, though the evidence base is uneven.
This methodological profile matters for interpreting the revision literature: descriptive accounts of uptake predominate over designs capable of isolating feedback type.
Direct corrections appear to support longer-term accuracy where metalinguistic codes do not.
Automated feedback occupies a different position in the revision process.
What the library does not yet establish is how revision behaviour differs when learners choose among feedback sources rather than receiving them in a fixed sequence [NEEDS CITATION].
Evidence on automated feedback remains largely corpus- or case-based, with limited classroom uptake data.
